newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi judge sets release of Liggett papers.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi judge sets release of Liggett papers.

text.p: A Mississippi judge ruled on Wednesday that internal documents from Brooke Group Ltd.'s Liggett Group could be turned over to plaintiffs in a $650 million second-hand smoke lawsuit against the U.S. tobacco industry.

Jones County Circuit Judge Billy Joe Landrum said 11 documents taken from five boxes of Liggett papers were not privileged information and could be seen by lawyers for the family of the late Burl Butler, a local barber who died of cancer in 1994.
But he stayed his order until Friday at 5 p.m. CST to give attorneys for the tobacco industry time to lodge an appeal with the Mississippi Supreme Court.

Proponents of the anti-tobacco movement hailed the ruling as an important victory. They speculated that the order, unless blocked by the high court, would turn some closely guarded industry secrets into public information for potential use in tobacco lawsuits across the country.

The Liggett documents were part of last week's settlement between the fifth largest U.S. cigarette maker and 22 state attorneys general. The states are suing the industry for an estimated $30 billion in Medicaid funds spent treating poor smokers.
"This is pretty historic. There's no question in my mind that these documents are going to see the light of day," said state Attorney General Mike Moore, who attended the hearing.
Landrum became the first judge to review the documents since last week's settlement, breaking off from the hearing for more than an hour to read them.
Judges in Florida, Texas and Illinois have ordered the documents to be turned over for possible use in state suits. But no ruling has made the papers available to plaintiffs, up to now.

Landrum also ordered that copies of the documents be forwarded under seal to Jackson County Chancery Court Judge Wiilliam Myers in Pascagoula, Miss. Myers is presiding over Mississippi's case to recoup nearly $1 billion Medicaid funds from cigarette makers.
Plaintiffs' attorneys believe the documents may contain information crucial to the Butler case.

The family contends that the 60-year-old Butler, who never smoked, died from the second-hand smoke he breathed from the cigarettes, cigars and pipes of people who patronised his Laurel, Miss., barber shop over the course of 30 years.
The suit alleges that cigarette makers knew of the dangers of smoking for decades but concealed the information from the public.
In response to a motion from the Butler family attorneys, Landrum concluded that the documents were only part of trial preparation not intended for testimony.

Ron Motley, a plaintiffs' attorney from Charleston, S.C., later said he believed the documents would show that cigarette makers destroyed papers to hide information both from other plaintiffs and from the public.
